Empirical Research Plan: “The Causal Effect of Medicare Eligibility at Age 65 on Mortality”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)

Rationale  
• The Medicare program generates an exogenous, sharp jump in legal eligibility at the exact 65th birthday.  
• Insurance take-up rises discretely but not from 0 → 1, so the first-stage is discontinuous but incomplete ⇒ “fuzzy.”  
• Given cross-sectional microdata with exact age in days/months and outcomes measured around the threshold, RDD isolates local causal effects under minimal assumptions of continuity.  
• Event studies or DiD would require stronger parallel-trend assumptions; IV would duplicate the fuzzy RDD estimator. Hence RDD is most credible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Running variable: AGE_i  = exact age in days (or months) relative to 65th birthday; 0 = 65 years.

Cutoff: c = 0 (turning 65).

Treatment indicator (eligibility): T_i  = 1{AGE_i ≥ 0}.  
Actual treatment (insurance coverage): M_i  = 1 if individual reports Medicare coverage.

Groups  
• Treatment group (just above cutoff): individuals with AGE in [0, h].  
• Control group (just below cutoff): individuals with AGE in [−h, 0).  
h is the chosen bandwidth.

Timing: Cross-sectional snapshots; outcomes are 1-year mortality (death within 12 months after survey interview) or similar short-horizon rates to stay “local.”

First-stage: ΔE[M_i | AGE=c]  
Reduced form: ΔE[Y_i | AGE=c] where Y = mortality.  
Local Wald (fuzzy RDD): τ_RD = (discontinuity in mortality)/(discontinuity in coverage).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Continuity of potential outcomes: In the absence of Medicare, the conditional expectation of potential mortality is smooth through age 65. Highly plausible—biological aging is continuous.  
2. No precise manipulation of running variable: Individuals cannot alter their actual date of birth; sample inclusion based on age in survey cannot be strategically changed. Plausible.  
3. Single treatment discontinuity: No other policies create an equally sharp jump exactly at 65 that directly affects mortality. Some retirement incentives co-incide but are smoother; we will test robustness (see Threats).  
4. Stable compositional density: The density of age near 65 is continuous (testable via McCrary).  
5. Local treatment homogeneity: The causal effect is constant within the chosen bandwidth (standard in RDD).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Simultaneous socio-economic changes at age 65 (retirement, Social Security claiming) may affect mortality directly.  
• Mitigation: (i) Control for labor-force status/earnings; (ii) narrow bandwidth (±6 months) where labor-force exit is more gradual; (iii) placebo tests at 64 & 66 where Social Security claiming changes less sharply.

Threat 2: Differential survey timing—interviews on birthdays just after 65 may capture different seasons (mortality seasonality).  
• Mitigation: Include month-of-interview fixed effects; run “donut” RDD excluding ±2 weeks around the cutoff.

Threat 3: Age heaping / misreporting near 65.  
• Mitigation: Use NHIS continuous age in months (exact date of birth). Perform McCrary test; if evidence of bunching at whole years, re-estimate using age-in-days supplied in MCBS, or implement heaping-adjusted weights.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --- 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)       # fast estimators
library(rdrobust)     # RDD
library(rddensity)    # McCrary
# ------------------------------------------------------------------

# --- 1. Load data --------------------------------------------------
nhis   <- read_csv("NHIS_merged.csv")   # contains age_in_days, medicare, dead_12m, covariates
mcbs   <- read_csv("MCBS_merged.csv")   # optional for robustness

# keep only NHIS for main spec
df <- nhis %>%
  mutate(age_rel65 = age_in_days - 65*365.25,   # running var centered at 0
         elig65    = if_else(age_rel65 >= 0, 1, 0),
         mortality = dead_12m)

# --- 2. Density & covariate checks --------------------------------
rddensity(df$age_rel65, c = 0)                    # McCrary test
covs <- c("sex","race","education","state")       # Balance check
for (v in covs) {
  print(feols(as.formula(paste(v,"~ elig65 | 0")), 
              data = df %>% filter(abs(age_rel65) < 365)))
}

# --- 3. Main fuzzy RDD (local linear, IK bandwidth) ---------------
main_rd <- rdrobust(y = df$mortality,
                    x = df$age_rel65,
                    c = 0,
                    fuzzy = df$medicare)          # instrumented by elig65 internally
summary(main_rd)

# --- 4. Alternative bandwidth & polynomial robustness -------------
robust_rd <- rdrobust(y = df$mortality,
                      x = df$age_rel65,
                      c = 0,
                      p = 2,                       # quadratic
                      h = 180)                     # ±6 months
summary(robust_rd)

# --- 5. Placebo cutoff at 64 --------------------------------------
placebo_rd <- rdrobust(y = df$mortality,
                       x = df$age_rel65,
                       c = -365,                   # 64th birthday
                       fuzzy = df$medicare)
summary(placebo_rd)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic/clinical intuition suggests Medicare coverage improves access to care, potentially lowering short-run mortality. Prior quasi-experimental evidence finds a 0.1–0.3 ppt (10–30 bps) drop in one-year mortality at 65. I expect a negative effect of roughly −0.2 percentage points (≈ 3–5 % relative decline from a 4 ppt baseline mortality in this age cell).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: No precise manipulation of running variable ………………… 1  
C2: Continuity of potential outcomes at cutoff ………………… 1  
C3: Correct functional form / bandwidth verified ……………… 0.8 (score 1→ use multiple h & p)  
C4: Absence of other simultaneous discontinuities …………… 0.5  
C5: Robust measurement & outcome definition ………………… 0.8  

Overall ≈ 4.1 / 5.
